title: Learning to arrange from Gus Wilson; Benny Carter
summary: Edison began writing in the early 1940s, learning voicing from Gus Wilson in Jeter-Pillars, and admires Benny Carter for writing as well as he plays.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Well, when did you start writing arrangements?

Oh, I started in the '40s. '42, '43, you know. I wrote, "Every Tug," and "I Sent for You Yesterday," "Jive at Five," that's mine. Oh, quite a few of the tunes that were recorded in those days were mine, you know.
Well, how did you pick up that skill? How did you do that?
Well, when I was in Jeeter-Pillar's band, Gus Johnson and I, we became very good friends and he was a fantastic writer. Beautiful arranger.

Yeah, Gus, Teddy's brother. So I used to ask him, you know, how do you put the trombone here, how you put the trumpets here, how you voice the altos, you know, the E flat scale, different than the B flat scale. And he used to tell me to put the note here and put the note there and experiment. After you hear it one time, change it. Put it in a different perspective, a different place.
So I started doing that and it sounded pretty good sometimes. But, you know, after hearing Benny Carter and guys like that write, you know, I finally got so --
Yeah, but some of those things were --

Yeah, but I got discouraged. And I loved to play. I loved to play. I only know one man that writes equally as well as he plays, that's Benny Carter. Benny can play and he can write, both. He's superb with both, you know. I mean, go out and make a living at either one, he can. He can go out and make a living playing and forget about writing and he can put his horn down and forget about his horn and pick up the pen and pencil.
